title: Files, pages and records
lead: File organisation, fixed and variable-length pages, slotted pages and record representation.

sections.title: Database files and heap files
sections.html:
Logical files and record access

A table is stored as a logical database file, which consists of pages holding records. The file layer offers file creation/deletion, record insertion/deletion/update, RID lookup and scan with an optional predicate. The disk manager transfers opaque page bytes; the buffer manager controls residency; the file layer interprets records within those bytes.

Heap files impose no key order, unlike sorted or index-organised files. A heap file is unrelated to the heap priority-queue data structure. Growing and shrinking it requires tracking member pages, free space and record locations.

PDF pp. 1–7

Linked lists versus a page directory

The linked-list design has a header and separate lists for full pages and pages with free space. A new record may require walking many partly free pages before finding enough bytes; “non-full” does not mean “large enough for this record”.

A directory entry instead records page ID and available bytes. Many page descriptors fit in one directory page, often cached, so the system can select a target without reading each candidate data page. The directory consumes extra metadata space and must be updated when free space changes.

PDF pp. 8–9

sections.title: Fixed-length page layouts
sections.html:
Packed fixed-length pages

A page header can contain its ID, record count, free-space offsets and links. For fixed-size records, record i begins at H+(i−1)L, with header length H and record length L. Appending record n+1 writes at H+nL.

In the source page, records A,B,C,D occupy consecutive slots; insertion appends E as slot 5. Deleting B can move E into slot 2. This preserves a packed region but changes E’s position-based RID from (page,5) to (page,2), potentially invalidating indexes or references. Updating a record in place works only while its size remains compatible with the allocated position.

PDF pp. 10–16

Unpacked bitmap and free-list pages

A bitmap marks occupied versus free fixed-size slots. Deleting B clears its bit; inserting a later record finds a zero bit and reuses that slot. Other slot positions remain stable.

A free list stores next-free links in unused slots. Insertion removes the head; deletion puts the released slot at the head and links it to the old head. The source’s deletion of C illustrates this pointer update. These schemes avoid moving unrelated records but retain holes and spend metadata on free-slot management.

PDF pp. 17–19

sections.title: Variable-length records and slotted pages
sections.html:
Slotted-page insert, delete and compaction

Variable record lengths prevent arithmetic lookup by one constant stride. A slot directory supplies indirection: RID=(page ID,slot ID), and each slot gives the current record offset. Slots and record bytes typically grow towards one another from opposite page ends.

Deletion marks a slot invalid (−1 in the slide). A nonfinal slot is retained so the IDs of later slots do not shift. Insertion reuses an invalid slot or creates one and reserves exactly the record’s bytes. Fragmentation can leave enough total free bytes but no contiguous area; compaction moves record bytes and updates slot offsets. The live record’s RID stays stable because its slot ID does not change.

PDF pp. 20–23

sections.title: Record layout and NULL representation
sections.html:
Field offsets, delimiters and NULL

Schema types reside in the system catalog rather than being repeated in every record. Fixed fields use prefix sums of field sizes: for 4B,2B,8B,2B fields, the third starts six bytes from the record base, ignoring any record header.

Variable fields can use delimiters, requiring scans and escaping, or offsets/descriptors for direct access. Equal start/end offsets indicate an empty value but cannot alone distinguish NULL from an empty string. A NULL bitmap or equivalent tag records that distinction. Offset tables are useful even with fixed-size fields when representation choices vary.

PDF pp. 24–27

The source byte layout

Record: (12344, Jones, CS, 18)
byte  0..7 : bigint sid
byte  8..11: (offset=21, length=5) for name
byte 12..15: (offset=26, length=2) for dept
byte 16..19: integer age
byte 20    : NULL bitmap
byte 21..25: Jones
byte 26..27: CS

The offsets are relative to this record, and their units are bytes. Fixed-size descriptors allow the DBMS to locate variable strings without scanning prior values. This example links table values to record bytes, then records to slots, pages and files.

PDF pp. 28–29

quiz.question: In the slotted-page example, must the index change the RID when the record in slot 2 moves?
options: No, if the slot ID remains unchanged
The RID is a byte offset, so the record cannot move
quiz.explanation: The slot directory updates the byte offset. The index still finds the record through (page 9, slot 2).
